Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old woman with a 3-day history of a severe, predominantly right periorbital/diffuse headache (8/10) with photophobia, transient “shooting lights,” nausea/feeling sick, and poor response to ibuprofen; clinician considers probable acute migraine and discussed escalation of analgesia and follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Severe headache for ~3 days; started gradually at work and worsened over the first 48 hours.
  - Pain diffuse but mainly around the right eye; described as generally dull with intermittent sharper episodes.
  - Severity reported as 8/10.
- Timeline / progression:
  - Onset ~3 days ago while at work; worsened overnight and has been present continuously with fluctuating intensity.
  - Took ibuprofen for the last 2 days with minimal benefit.
- Exacerbating / relieving factors:
  - Bright lights and screen use aggravate symptoms; patient reduced screen brightness with some relief.
  - Dehydration and stress were considered by patient as possible triggers.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Photophobia: “light is quite annoying, it hurts.”
  - Transient visual phenomena at onset described as “weird shooting lights.”
  - Nausea / “feeling sick”; no vomiting.
  - Difficulty focusing; required time off work.
  - No fever, no rash, no neck stiffness, no speech disturbance, no limb weakness, no recent head injury.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No prior diagnosis of migraine (patient reports she has not had migraines herself).
  - No vomiting, no vision loss, no focal neurological deficits reported.

Past Medical History:
- Patient reports otherwise “fit and well”; no chronic medical conditions documented.
- No personal history of migraines (family history positive—see below).

Medications:
- Recent/OTC:
  - Ibuprofen: patient reports taking approximately 3 tablets per day for the last 2 days; dose per tablet and route/frequency details not fully documented.
- Regular medications: none reported.
- Allergies: none known / “not that I know of.”

Social History:
- Lives with three housemates.
- Occupation: works in IT; prolonged computer/screen use.
- Vision: wears glasses since childhood; no recent eye test reported.
- Tobacco: smokes socially.
- Alcohol: drinks socially.
- Contraceptive status: asked but not clearly documented in transcript.

Family History:
- Mother and sister have frequent migraines (mother’s migraines can be severe and disabling).

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Exam findings: Not recorded (no focused neurological exam documented in transcript).

Investigations:
- None ordered or reported in the encounter.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Probable acute migraine (most likely) presenting with unilateral-predominant periorbital/diffuse headache, photophobia, transient visual phenomena, and associated nausea; poor response to current OTC ibuprofen. Secondary causes not suspected acutely given absence of red flags, but to be monitored.

DDx Integration (top items consistent with transcript):
1) Migraine headache (probable acute migraine) — Supporting: unilateral periorbital predominance; photophobia; transient visual “shooting lights” (possible aura); nausea; strong family history; poor response to OTC analgesia. Opposing: patient reports no prior personal history of migraine; pain described mainly dull rather than classically throbbing.
2) Tension-type headache / stress-related headache — Supporting: dull, diffuse quality; recent work stress and prolonged screen use; partial relief with reduced screen brightness and previous response to ibuprofen. Opposing: photophobia, visual phenomena, and significant nausea are less typical.
3) Eyestrain / uncorrected refractive error — Supporting: longstanding glasses, prolonged IT/screen work, relief with reduced screen brightness and report of difficulty focusing. Opposing: “shooting lights,” photophobia, and nausea favor migraine.

Issue 1: Acute severe headache — probable migraine
- Assessment:
  - Probable acute migraine based on history (photophobia, transient visual phenomena, nausea, unilateral-predominant periorbital pain, family history).
- Plan:
  - Optimize analgesia: clinician discussed options including optimizing ibuprofen dosing (clinician advised patient can take up to two tablets three times daily — dosing reviewed in encounter), and offering alternative/stronger anti-inflammatory (naproxen) and/or addition of paracetamol or codeine; clinician discussed prescribing stronger analgesia today (prescription discussed).
  - Symptomatic measures: reduce screen brightness, rest in a dark environment, consider antiemetic if nausea worsens (antiemetic not explicitly prescribed in transcript).
  - Headache diary recommended to identify triggers and frequency.
  - Arrange follow-up in 1–2 weeks to reassess; earlier review if symptoms worsen or become more frequent to consider prophylactic therapy.

Issue 2: Rule out secondary/serious causes (e.g., SAH, meningitis, intracranial process)
- Assessment:
  - No red-flag features documented (no thunderclap onset, no neck stiffness, no fever, no focal neurological deficits, no vomiting). Serious secondary causes considered unlikely at present but remain on differential if course changes.
- Plan:
  - No immediate imaging or labs documented/ordered during this visit.
  - Safety-netting: return urgently or call if new or worsening neurological signs (vision loss, persistent/ progressive weakness, speech difficulty), severe deterioration, persistent vomiting, or signs of systemic infection.
  - If headaches become recurrent, atypical, or progressive despite treatment, consider further investigation (neuroimaging/neurology referral) — to be decided at follow-up (discussion of further workup implied by differential but not ordered today).

Issue 3: Eyestrain / refractive error contribution
- Assessment:
  - Possible contribution from prolonged screen use and outdated refractive correction.
- Plan:
  - Recommend formal eye test / optometry review given long interval since last test.
  - Continue ergonomic measures (screen brightness reduction, breaks from screen), reassess effect on headaches.

General plan items:
- Consider short-term prescription of stronger analgesia as discussed (naproxen, or combination paracetamol/codeine) — prescription discussed by clinician during visit.
- Keep headache diary and return for planned follow-up in 1–2 weeks or sooner for worsening/new neurological symptoms.
- Discuss prophylactic migraine therapy if headaches become frequent on follow-up.

Quality checks:
- Missing/expected items not documented: vitals, focused neurological examination, contraception status (pill), exact ibuprofen dose per tablet and full medication route/dosing details, whether a prescription was actually provided (clinician offered to prescribe).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none identified; DDx supports clinician’s probable migraine impression (no direct contradictions). 
- Transcript quality: clear audio and complete history; some questions (contraception) were not clearly answered/documented.
